Let's recall the binomial theorem for positive integer [MATH: n\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {(a + b)^n} = {n \choose 0}{a^n}{b^0} + {n \choose 1}{a^{n - 1}}{b^1} + {n \choose 2}{a^{n - 2}}{b^2} + \cdots + {n \choose n}{a^0}{b^n}]

Content:
If we substitute [MATH: a=1] and [MATH: b=x] into the binomial theorem, we obtain (after some manipulations)

Content:
[MATH: {(1 + x)^n} = 1 + nx + \dfrac{{n(n - 1)}}{{2!}}{x^2} + \dfrac{{n(n - 1)(n - 2)}}{{3!}}{x^3} +\cdots + x^n.]

sections.normalized_html: Determine the coefficient of [MATH: r^3] in the expansion of [MATH: \left( 1 - 3r \right)^{10}.]
sections.readable_text: Determine the coefficient of [MATH: r^3] in the expansion of [MATH: \left( 1 - 3r \right)^{10}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

The binomial expansion for [MATH: (1 + x)^n] is given by [MATH: (1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n - 1)}{2!} x^2 + \cdots .]

In particular, the [MATH: x^3] term is given by [MATH: \dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!} x^3.]

Replacing [MATH: x] with [MATH: -3r] and [MATH: n] with [MATH: 10] in the above expression, we get [MATH: (10(10 − 1)(10 − 2))/(3!)(− 3r)^{3}|= (10(9)(8))/(6) ⋅ (− 3)^{3} ⋅ r^{3}; = (10(9)(8))/(6) ⋅ (− 27)r^{3}; = − 3240r^{3}.]

Therefore, the coefficient of [MATH: r^3] is [MATH: -3\,240.]

Content:
Let's derive our special case formula from the binomial theorem for positive integer [MATH: n\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {(a + b)^n} = {n \choose 0}{a^n}{b^0} + {n \choose 1}{a^{n - 1}}{b^1} + {n \choose 2}{a^{n - 2}}{b^2} + {n \choose 3}{a^{n - 3}}{b^3} + \cdots + {n \choose n}{a^0}{b^n}]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: a=1] and [MATH: b=x] into the above, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: (1 + x)^{n}|= ((n)/(0)) ⋅ 1^{n} ⋅ x^{0} + ((n)/(1)) ⋅ 1^{n − 1} ⋅ x^{1} + ((n)/(2)) ⋅ 1^{n − 2} ⋅ x^{2} + ⋯ + ((n)/(n)) ⋅ 1^{0} ⋅ x^{n}; = ((n)/(0)) + ((n)/(1))x + ((n)/(2))x^{2} + ((n)/(3))x^{3} + ⋯ + ((n)/(n))x^{n}]

Content:
Now, recall that

Content:
[MATH: {n \choose r} = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\cdot r!}]

Content:
and the particular cases

Content:
[MATH: {n \choose 0} = 1, \qquad {n \choose 1} = n.]

Content:
We can now continue to simplify our binomial expansion as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (1 + x)^{n}|= ((n)/(0)) + ((n)/(1))x + ((n)/(2))x^{2} + ((n)/(3))x^{3} + ⋯ + ((n)/(n))x^{n}; = 1 + n ⋅ x + (n!)/((n − 2)! ⋅ 2!) ⋅ x^{2} + (n!)/((n − 3)! ⋅ 3!) ⋅ x^{3} + ⋯ + x^{n}; = 1 + n ⋅ x + (n(n − 1)(n − 2)!)/((n − 2)! ⋅ 2!) ⋅ x^{2} + (n(n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3)!)/((n − 3)! ⋅ 3!) ⋅ x^{3} + ⋯ + x^{n}; = 1 + n ⋅ x + (n(n − 1)(n − 2)!)/((n − 2)! ⋅ 2!) ⋅ x^{2} + (n(n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3)!)/((n − 3)! ⋅ 3!) ⋅ x^{3} + ⋯ + x^{n}; = 1 + nx + (n(n − 1))/(2!)x^{2} + (n(n − 1)(n − 2))/(3!)x^{3} + ⋯ + x^{n},]

Content:
which gives the desired result.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's recall the binomial theorem for positive integer [MATH: n\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {(a + b)^n} = {n \choose 0}{a^n}{b^0} + {n \choose 1}{a^{n - 1}}{b^1} + {n \choose 2}{a^{n - 2}}{b^2} + \cdots + {n \choose n}{a^0}{b^n}]

Content:
If we substitute [MATH: a=1] and [MATH: b=x] into the binomial theorem, we obtain (after some manipulations)

Content:
[MATH: {(1 + x)^n} = 1 + nx + \dfrac{{n(n - 1)}}{{2!}}{x^2} + \dfrac{{n(n - 1)(n - 2)}}{{3!}}{x^3} +\cdots + x^n.]

Content:
We'll derive this result at the end of the lesson.

Content:
It's often useful to use this version of the binomial formula whenever there is only one variable and the other term equals [MATH: 1.]

Item 2 — Example: Expanding a Binomial

[MATH: {(1 + x)^n} = 1 + nx + \frac{{n(n - 1)}}{{2!}}{x^2} + \cdots .]

By substituting [MATH: x=3a] and [MATH: n=5] into the above formula, we obtain
[MATH: (1 + 3a)^{5}|= 1 + 5(3a) + (5(5 − 1))/(2!)(3a)^{2} + ⋯; = 1 + 5(3a) + (5(4))/(2)(9a^{2}) + ⋯; = 1 + 15a + 90a^{2} + ⋯.]
